To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
pharmacological block and viral-mediated knockdown of HHCN channels in thalamus prevent absence seizures.

pharmacological and genetic suppression of hyperpolarization- activated cyclic nucleotide-gating (HCN) channel function in thalamoc cortical neurons prevents genetically determined and pharmacologically induced absence seizures.

the suppression of thalamocortically projecting neuron HCN channels via either pharmacological block or genetic knockdown leads to a marked decrease in absence seizures in two rodent models of genetic absence epilepsy and a rodent model of pharmacologically induced absence seizures.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the mechanisms of absence seizures, which is a common type of epilepsy that occurs during childhood and adolescence and is characterized by a loss of consciousness.
the identification of novel therapeutic targets for the treatment of absence seizures.
the role of HCN channels and the Ih currents they generate in the pathophysiological process of absence seizures.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thalamic HN channels are a key target to prevent AS generation.
HCN channels play an opposite role in cortical and thalaminic neuronal populations in the modulation of nonconvulsive absence seizures.
the role of Ih in the generation of ASs is complex and depends on the neuronal population and the genetic or pharmacological origin of the seizures.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
thalamocorticothalamic network activity is necessary for ASs generation, whereas cortical activity alone is not sufficient to generate ASs.
the thalamic Hcn channels play an essential role in the pathophysiology of absence seizures.
HCN channel function in TC neurons contributes to the pathogenesis of absence seizures.
